extracted.intended_audience: general encyclopedia readers; students and researchers interested in performance, race, and cultural history
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate performances in which makeup is used to make a performer appear white, including historical origins, notable examples, and comparisons with blackface. Useful for understanding when such performances are regarded as satire, art, or controversial/racist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of whiteface
rubrics_metrics.description: Whiteface is a type of performance in which a person of color uses makeup in order to appear fair-skinned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page frames the term as a reversal of blackface (makeup used to appear black) and identifies whiteface as specifically the use of makeup by a person of color to appear white.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical origin and precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Whiteface performances originated in the 19th century; early documented uses include minstrel/vaudeville contexts and stage impersonations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earliest citations noted (e.g., New York Clipper 1870, Dooley Wilson's Irishman impersonation, Canada Lee in 1947). Historical pedigree is relevant to classification and interpretation of the practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notable examples and media contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whiteface has appeared in films, television, music videos and reality TV, with examples including Watermelon Man, Eddie Murphy's SNL and film characters, White Chicks, Black. White., and various music-video/online skits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listing concrete examples helps identify common uses (comedy, undercover plot devices, character impressions) and situates modern occurrences in popular culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to blackface and linkage to historical oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackface is widely considered racist due to its traceable racial links to slavery and racial segregation; this historical linkage is a central reason for its condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whiteface, compare whether the performance draws upon the same kinds of historical stereotypes and oppressive legacy that make blackface offensive; absence or presence of that linkage is a key discriminator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent — satire/character impression vs. racist stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenders of whiteface often argue it is intended as satire or a character impression and does not draw on a legacy of racism in the way blackface does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess performer intent (satire, critique, impersonation) and whether the intended satire targets white lifestyles/privilege rather than perpetuating demeaning stereotypes of a marginalized group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary acceptability and context (comedic vs. condemned)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackface is heavily condemned in modern art forms, while whiteface is occasionally employed in modern times, usually in a comedic context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider current cultural norms and medium: whiteface may be tolerated or interpreted as comedy/satire in some contexts but reception varies; contemporary condemnation is a major factor in evaluating legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the transformation (narrative device, undercover, promotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whiteface has been used for specific narrative purposes (e.g., undercover plots), promotional character work, or satirical sketches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the makeup serves a clear narrative/character purpose (e.g., plot device in White Chicks, character impression on SNL) versus gratuitous or demeaning use; purposeful storytelling use may affect reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power dynamics and 'punching up' vs 'punching down' in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commentary frames whiteface as satire that 'punches up' at power rather than punching down at an oppressed group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whom the satire targets and whether it challenges power structures or reinforces oppression; satire aimed at powerful groups is often judged differently than satire that ridicules marginalized people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism and portrayal techniques (makeup realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whiteface performances often rely on makeup to realistically portray fair-skinned characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of realism, skill of makeup, and whether the portrayal leans into stereotyped mannerisms or caricature influence whether the performance is read as respectful impersonation or offensive caricature.
